title: I wept too much
hookLine: Seneca admits he grieved his friend Annaeus Serenus beyond measure (Letters 63)

lines: THEN SENECA TURNS THE LIGHT ON HIMSELF.
cards: Lucilius has lost a friend named Flaccus, and he's taking it hard. Seneca writes back with the advice a Stoic is supposed to give: grieve, but within measure. Don't let your eyes stay dry, and don't let them flood.
Weep, but don't wail. It's sensible and balanced. Then, near the end of the sixty-third letter, Seneca does something unexpected in a letter of advice.
He turns the light on himself, and tells his friend about the time he didn't follow his own advice at all.

teach.b: Seneca's rule for grief sits in the middle: let the eyes be neither dry nor overflowing. Tears are natural. Endless, performed grief, he thinks, often has more to do with being seen to grieve than with the friend.

teach.h: I WEPT FOR SERENUS BEYOND MEASURE.
teach.b: I write this to you, he says, I who wept for my dear friend Annaeus Serenus so far beyond measure that, against my will, I'm one of the examples of people conquered by grief.
Serenus was younger than Seneca, and a close friend.

teach.h: I NEVER THOUGHT HE'D GO FIRST.
teach.b: Seneca had never once considered that Serenus might die first. He'd thought only of their ages, as if death went in order. Now, he says, I condemn myself for that, because I didn't think it could happen.
A teacher who'd never failed his own rule would be easier to admire and harder to trust.

teach.h: THE STUMBLE MAKES THE RULE HUMAN.
teach.b: Seneca gives Lucilius the rule and the stumble together, and the stumble makes the rule human.

Looking back on the week, from the dark house to the seasick swim to the tunnel, the man keeps telling stories against himself. The lesson isn't don't weep. It's: weep, and don't pretend it couldn't happen.

how: Readers of Seneca often take from this letter permission to grieve honestly, and to admit when grief has overflowed their own expectations.

o: Latin for the grief people perform in order to be seen
Latin for a Roman funeral song sung for a friend
Latin for tears, which Seneca let overflow for Serenus

games.q: the sixty-third letter — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca says a Stoic should never cry
his rule is: neither dry eyes nor overflowing ones.
Seneca admits he grieved Serenus beyond his own rule
he calls himself an example of someone conquered by grief.
he was younger, which is why Seneca never imagined he'd die first.

games.q: you're Seneca, advising a grieving friend to keep his grief in measure. you once failed this yourself. what do you do?
o: leave that out: it weakens the advice.
tell him plainly that you wept beyond measure for Serenus.
games.why: Seneca confesses it in the same letter, and names his mistake: never imagining the younger friend could go first.

practice: Go gently here; if a loss is very fresh, simply breathe and rest instead.
Otherwise, bring to mind one person or thing you've lost and let yourself feel whatever is there, sadness, anger, numbness, even relief, without measuring it.
If tears come, let them; if not, that's fine too, and breathe with the loss as you'd sit with a friend.

wordCard.voice: Lacrimae. Latin for tears: Seneca confesses he wept for his friend Serenus far beyond his own rule that grief stay neither dry nor overflowing. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: tears. Letters 63.1 asks that the eyes be neither dry nor overflowing.
